questions.prompt: The simplest op-amp model (a voltage-controlled voltage source) with input resistance \(R_{in}\), gain \(A\) and output resistance \(R_{out}\) captures which imperfections?
options: Only the frequency dependence of the gain
Slew rate and offset voltage as well as finite gain
Nothing: it is exactly the ideal op-amp
Finite gain \(A\), finite input resistance and non-zero output resistance, but NOT frequency dependence
questions.explanation:
The VCVS model has \(v_{out}=A\,v_{in}\) behind \(R_{out}\), with \(R_{in}\) across the input (reader Fig. 17.8). It is a linear, frequency-independent model, so it cannot describe gain falling with frequency (that needs the \(R_x\)-\(C_x\) node), slew rate, or offsets.
• The ideal op-amp is the limit \(A\to\infty\), \(R_{in}\to\infty\), \(R_{out}\to0\) of this same model.

questions.prompt: In terms of the VCVS model parameters \(A\), \(R_{in}\), \(R_{out}\), the IDEAL op-amp is the limit
options: \(A\to0\), \(R_{in}\to0\), \(R_{out}\to\infty\)
\(A\to\infty\), \(R_{in}\to0\), \(R_{out}\to\infty\)
\(A\to\infty\), \(R_{in}\to\infty\), \(R_{out}\to0\)
\(A\to1\), \(R_{in}\to\infty\), \(R_{out}\to0\)
questions.explanation:
An ideal voltage amplifier draws no input current (\(R_{in}=\infty\)), produces its output regardless of the load (\(R_{out}=0\)), and has unlimited gain so that the input difference is driven to zero in feedback (\(A=\infty\)).
The other combinations describe a poor amplifier: low \(R_{in}\) loads the source, high \(R_{out}\) loses gain into a load.

questions.prompt: In the single-pole op-amp model (figure), an ideal transconductor with \(G_m=2\ \mathrm{mS}\) drives a node with \(R_x=500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) in parallel with \(C_x\). What is the DC gain \(A_0=G_mR_x\)?
questions.explanation:
At DC the capacitor is an open circuit, so the current \(G_m v_d\) flows only through \(R_x\): \(v_x=G_mR_xv_d\). Thus \(A_0=G_mR_x=2\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S}\times5\times10^{5}\ \Omega=1000\) (reader Eq. 17.15).
The unity buffer after the node doesn't change the gain.

questions.prompt: An op-amp model has \(G_m=1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_x=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\), \(C_x=5\ \mathrm{pF}\). What is the open-loop \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency \(f_{-3\mathrm{dB}}\), in kHz?
questions.explanation:
The node impedance is \(R_x\parallel C_x\), a single pole at \(\omega_{-3dB}=\dfrac{1}{R_xC_x}=\dfrac{1}{10^{6}\cdot5\times10^{-12}}=2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) (reader Eq. 17.16).
In hertz, divide by \(2\pi\): \(f_{-3dB}=31.83\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Common mistake: leaving the answer in rad/s (200 krad/s).

questions.prompt: For the same model (\(G_m=1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_x=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\), \(C_x=5\ \mathrm{pF}\)), what is the gain-bandwidth product \(A_0\cdot f_{-3\mathrm{dB}}\), in MHz?
questions.explanation:
\(A_0=G_mR_x=1000\) and \(f_{-3dB}=31.83\ \mathrm{kHz}\), so \(A_0f_{-3dB}=31.83\ \mathrm{MHz}\).
Equivalently \(\omega_u=\dfrac{G_m}{C_x}=\dfrac{10^{-3}}{5\times10^{-12}}=2\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), i.e. \(f_u=\dfrac{G_m}{2\pi C_x}\): \(R_x\) cancels out of the product (reader Eq. 17.17).

questions.prompt: In the single-pole model, \(R_x\) is doubled while \(G_m\) and \(C_x\) stay the same. What happens to the DC gain \(A_0\) and the gain-bandwidth product?
options: \(A_0\) doubles and the gain-bandwidth product doubles
\(A_0\) doubles, the pole halves, and the gain-bandwidth product is unchanged
\(A_0\) is unchanged and the pole halves
\(A_0\) halves and the gain-bandwidth product halves
questions.explanation:
\(A_0=G_mR_x\) doubles. The pole \(\omega_{-3dB}=1/(R_xC_x)\) halves. The product \(A_0\,\omega_{-3dB}=G_m/C_x\) does not contain \(R_x\), so it stays put: more DC gain is bought with less bandwidth.
• GBW is set by \(G_m\) and \(C_x\) only.

questions.prompt: A model has the transconductor \(G_m\) feeding only a capacitor \(C_x\) (there is no \(R_x\)), followed by an ideal buffer. What is true of its open-loop gain?
options: The DC gain is infinite (it is an integrator), yet the unity-gain frequency is still \(\omega_u=G_m/C_x\)
The gain is zero at DC and rises at 20 dB/decade
The unity-gain frequency is infinite, since \(R_x\to\infty\)
The model has no frequency dependence
questions.explanation:
With no resistor, DC current has nowhere to go but into \(C_x\): \(v_x=\dfrac{G_mv_d}{j\omega C_x}\), so \(A(j\omega)=\dfrac{G_m}{j\omega C_x}=\dfrac{\omega_u}{j\omega}\). The gain is infinite as \(\omega\to0\), falls at \(-20\) dB/decade, and equals 1 at \(\omega_u=G_m/C_x\) (reader Fig. 17.12 and Eq. 17.17).
This is the high-frequency form \(A\approx\omega_u/j\omega\) of any single-pole op-amp, extended down to DC.

questions.prompt: A source with \(R_s=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) drives an amplifier modeled by \(R_{in}=9\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), a VCVS \(A\,v_{in}\) with \(A=1000\), and \(R_{out}=100\ \Omega\), loaded by \(R_L=300\ \Omega\). What is the overall gain \(v_{out}/v_s\)?
questions.explanation:
Two resistive dividers hide the gain loss. Input: \(v_{in}=v_s\dfrac{R_{in}}{R_s+R_{in}}=0.9\,v_s\). Output: \(v_{out}=A\,v_{in}\dfrac{R_L}{R_L+R_{out}}=A\,v_{in}\times0.75\).
Overall: \(0.9\times1000\times0.75=675\) V/V, 32.5% below the 'open' gain \(A=1000\). Common mistake: reading \(A=1000\) as the gain with a source and load attached.

questions.prompt: Real op-amps place an output buffer after the input transconductance (OTA) stage. Why?
options: The buffer adds extra voltage gain of 1000
The buffer removes the dominant pole
The OTA produces a voltage, which the buffer converts to a current
The OTA stage has a very high output impedance, so a resistive load would collapse its gain; the buffer provides low output impedance
questions.explanation:
The OTA converts the input voltage difference to a CURRENT into a high-impedance node (\(R_x\) and \(C_x\)); that node cannot drive a low-resistance load without its voltage collapsing (reader Sec. 17.4.5). The unity-gain buffer copies the node voltage and drives the load with a small \(R_{out}\).
• The buffer's gain is 1 (+1 in the figure), not 1000.
• The pole belongs to \(R_xC_x\) and stays in the model.
• The OTA output is a current; the buffer takes a voltage.

questions.prompt: Preview of gain-bandwidth. The model with \(G_m=1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(C_x=5\ \mathrm{pF}\) has \(f_u=G_m/2\pi C_x=31.83\ \mathrm{MHz}\). It is placed in a non-inverting amplifier with \(f=0.1\) (ideal gain 10). A later skill shows that the closed-loop bandwidth is \(f\cdot f_u\). What is it, in MHz?
questions.explanation:
The loop gain at DC is \(T_0=A_0f\), and feedback extends the pole by \(1+T_0\) (previous skills), giving \(\approx A_0 f\cdot f_{-3dB}=f\cdot f_u\). So \(BW_{closed}=0.1\times31.83\ \mathrm{MHz}=3.183\ \mathrm{MHz}\).
Gain 10 times the bandwidth 3.18 MHz = 31.8 MHz: the same gain-bandwidth product \(G_m/2\pi C_x\) as before. (Exactly, \((1+A_0f)f_{-3dB}=101\times31.83\ \mathrm{kHz}=3.21\ \mathrm{MHz}\); the 1% difference is within tolerance.) Reader note: Eq. 17.29 prints \(\omega_0=fT\) but should read \(\omega_0=f\,\omega_u\) (\(T=Gf\) already contains \(f\)).

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. In the model, the OTA current can never exceed \(I_{max}=100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). For a big input step the OTA saturates and charges \(C_x=5\ \mathrm{pF}\) at constant current. How fast does the internal node ramp?
options: \(2\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(200\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(20\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
\(0.02\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\)
questions.explanation:
A constant current into a capacitor gives a linear ramp: \(\dfrac{dv_x}{dt}=\dfrac{I_{max}}{C_x}=\dfrac{100\ \mu\mathrm{A}}{5\ \mathrm{pF}}=2\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{V/s}=20\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\) (reader Eq. 18.23).
Unit check: \(10^{-4}/(5\times10^{-12})=2\times10^7\), and \(1\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}=10^6\ \mathrm{V/s}\). The other choices are powers-of-ten slips. This 'speed limit' is the op-amp's slew rate.

questions.prompt: Preview of offset voltage. Real op-amps behave as if a small DC source \(V_{os}\) sits in series with one input of an offset-free amplifier. With both inputs grounded (open loop, \(A_0=1000\) at DC) and \(V_{os}=2\ \mathrm{mV}\), what is \(v_o\)?
questions.explanation:
The offset source adds directly to the differential input: \(v_d=V_{os}-0\). The model then gives \(v_o=A_0\,v_d=1000\times2\ \mathrm{mV}=2\ \mathrm{V}\).
An 'ideal' model would say \(v_o=0\) for zero input. Real op-amps with 1000× gain turn a 2 mV mismatch into 2 V (and with \(A=10^5\) would rail out), which is why offset is modeled and nulled. The next skills show how feedback tames it.
